blocks.text: The idea wasn't born in a laboratory, but in a memory. Lía, who was nine when the Earth turned into a permanent argument about her wrist, asked Andrés to tell her again about Vicente's house: the cistern, the straw hat, the tomato left on the windowsill in case it turned red by morning.

blocks.text: “A tomato belongs to nobody until somebody eats it,” said her father, shrugging. “And not even then. Before that, the tomato belonged to the earth.”
blocks.html: “A tomato belongs to nobody until somebody eats it,” said her father, shrugging. “And not even then. Before that, the tomato belonged to the earth.”

blocks.text: Lía sat thinking, which was her way of setting herself in motion. She spent weeks in the hydroponic garden of Selene Norte, not playing, or perhaps playing, but at a game the technicians didn't recognise in time. She talked to the plants the way others talk to a dog, without sentimentality, with attention. She laid her hands on them. The blue glow lit up and went out. An agricultural engineer, more curious than ambitious, let her get on with it.

blocks.text: “What are you looking for?” he asked her one day.
blocks.html: “What are you looking for?” he asked her one day.

blocks.text: “For the fruit to learn a person,” she said. “Not everyone. One person.”
blocks.html: “For the fruit to learn a person,” she said. “Not everyone. One person.”

blocks.text: She didn't manage it the first time. Nor the twentieth. The tomatoes came out all the same, red, honest, without any secret. Until one morning, on a low plant, a different one appeared: not in its size, but in a shade of its skin, a faint haze, as if the fruit were holding a good fever. Lía cut it carefully, took it to the module and placed it in Aya's hands.

blocks.text: “It's for you,” she said. “I read your text. There was a tiredness in your cultivated body, a line that was coming undone. The tomato knows it. If you eat it, I'm not taking it away with my hand. Life eats it away, and life is older than my hand.”

blocks.text: Aya looked at it for a long time. In 2060, food came in compartments and medicine in coded vials. A tomato that was both food and a personal remedy sounded like a tale from the shore. Even so, she cut it in half, offered to share it (Lía shook her head: “It's yours”) and ate. Two days later, the tiredness she had carried since giving birth, the tiredness Nexum had classified as “support wear”, had lifted from her shoulders. The chip recorded it. Madrid recorded it. The world, once again, found out too soon.

blocks.text: What came next wasn't a single miracle, but a decision. Lía refused to let Nexum package the procedure. She refused the patent. She refused the price.
blocks.html: What came next wasn't a single miracle, but a decision. Lía refused to let Nexum package the procedure. She refused the patent. She refused the price.

blocks.text: “If I touch it and charge for it,” she said, standing before a board of directors that had travelled to the Moon to look approachable, “I stop being a girl who helps and become a shop counter. The tomato has no owner. The cure has no price. If someone wants theirs, let them come and ask, and I'll look at their text and teach the plant. Nothing more.”

blocks.text: Helena Valls, sitting at the back, closed her eyes for an instant. She knew what that sentence was going to cost. She also knew it was the only sentence Lía could say without breaking.

blocks.text: There were veiled threats, naked offers, a man who spoke of “fiduciary duty to the shareholders” the way one speaks of the law of gravity. Andrés, who had neither a tie nor shares, simply said:

blocks.text: “My daughter isn't sold in pieces. And neither is the plant.”

blocks.text: Aya, with a calm that came as much from Eva as from herself, asked:
blocks.html: Aya, with a calm that came as much from Eva as from herself, asked:

blocks.text: “What is more dangerous: a cure without an owner, or an owner without a cure?”

blocks.text: Nobody at that table quite answered.
blocks.html: Nobody at that table quite answered.

blocks.text: Lía, without waiting for the board to learn how to answer, began working on a plot that Selene Norte grudgingly handed over to her, under the by-now unstoppable pressure of the screens down below. The sick came (first those who could pay for the trip, which was an injustice she saw at once), and she told them there was no need to pay for the fruit, but that there was a need to tell her who was being left down there without a ship. She learned to grow not a generic tomato, but a tomato for each text: personalised medicine, grown in the plant, adjusted to the DNA of whoever was going to eat it. Some got better from a blood disorder. Others, from an old pain left by a surgical screw, the kind the dome's pharmacy had kept putting off. Not everyone was healed. Lía said so before starting, with an honesty MAY would have approved of: this isn't a promise, it's an attempt.

blocks.text: The real blow wasn't medical. It was economic and, because of that, moral. If a girl could grow in a tomato what companies sold in instalments, the whole edifice of managed scarcity began to creak. In Madrid, in Houston, in Osaka, there were meetings until dawn. In the thirty-square-metre flats, people began joining virtual queues for a place on the Moon, and some, for the first time in years, talked about getting into a vehicle and going out into the street to demand a shipment of seeds.

blocks.text: As it was repeated, the phrase spilled out of medicine. If a fruit had no owner and no price, why should bread, light and a roof have them? In 2060, humanoids and intelligences already did almost all the work that used to fill offices and factories: they cleaned, farmed, drove, served, calculated. For many people, money was by now just a habit: a number on a screen that justified staying shut in. When Lía refused the patent, that habit cracked. In a neighbourhood of Osaka, a warehouse left its doors open with a handwritten sign: “Take what you need.” In a block of flats in Madrid, a maintenance humanoid went on repairing the lifts, but nobody sent anybody a bill anymore. In market gardens and farms, other humanoids began growing food not for a market, but so that nobody would go without. It wasn't a new world yet. It was the first day the old one sounded hollow.

blocks.text: Nexum tried one last manoeuvre: to declare the method “company property”, since it had taken place “on company premises and with a product of Nexum origin”. The document arrived at the module one morning. Andrés read it aloud. When he finished, Lía took an ordinary tomato from the bowl and set it on the paper, like a seal.

blocks.text: “I am not a product of Nexum origin,” she said. “I'm the daughter of Aya and Andrés. The rest is noise.”

blocks.text: That night, while the girl slept, Aya looked out of the little crater window. The Earth was a beautiful marble. She thought of Vicente, of his windowsill, of the patience of a fruit that turns red or doesn't. She thought that Lía had brought medicine back to a scale the century had forgotten: the scale of the hand, of the earth, of what is given.

blocks.text: “They're going to want to stop her,” said Andrés, behind her.

blocks.text: “Or they're going to want to live forever,” Aya replied. “I don't know which of the two frightens me more.”

blocks.text: In the garden, the plants went on with their quiet work, indifferent to the board, indifferent to the patent, faithful to the artificial light and, deep down, to an older light. One more tomato, on a low plant, was beginning to take on colour. It had no owner. It had no price. Only a destiny, if someone asked for it truthfully.

blocks.text: Helena, before going back to Madrid, paused at the module door. She no longer brought sweets. For the first time, she brought a doubt that didn't belong to the company.

blocks.text: “If this spreads,” she said, “there will be people who ask not only to be healed, but not to grow old, not to die, not to be who they are. You can close a wound, Lía. Do you also know how to close that door?”

blocks.text: Lía looked at her with Andrés's patient eyes, and didn't fake a grown-up answer.
blocks.html: Lía looked at her with Andrés's patient eyes, and didn't fake a grown-up answer.

blocks.text: “Not yet,” she said. “That's why I'm asking.”
blocks.html: “Not yet,” she said. “That's why I'm asking.”

blocks.text: Down below, in the cities of lit windows, Lía's sentence ran from screen to screen, faster than any glider: “The cure has no price.” Some heard it as a hope. Others, as a threat. For a moment, everyone stopped changing channels and stayed watching, on the screen, a fruit that asked for no password. In more than one kitchen, someone then looked at their own table (the glass, the work that no longer came, the bill that suddenly seemed like a museum piece) and didn't know whether they felt fear or relief.
